input_signals.name: margin_up_capex_down_trend
input_signals.expression: SUB(RANK(TREND(RATIO(ebitda, at), 5)), RANK(TREND(RATIO(capx, at), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms whose profitability is trending up while capital-expenditure intensity is trending down are harvesting mature, high-return franchises with improving efficiency; the opposite pattern (falling margins, rising capex intensity) signals capital being sunk into deteriorating economics and is overpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: Using five-year trends rather than levels captures the direction of the profitability/investment tradeoff, a state the market updates slowly because it requires linking two separate financial statements over time. The rank difference isolates the divergence between the two trends, which is inherently a cross-theme quantity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( rank( trend( ratio( ebitda, at ), 5 ) ), rank( trend( ratio( capx, at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: profit_weighted_low_reinvestment
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, MAX(oancf, dp)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What identifies the underpriced cash cow is not free cash flow per se but the share of internally generated cash that management chooses not to plow back: firms with strong cash profitability that reinvest only a small fraction of it are harvesting, while equally profitable firms reinvesting multiples of their cash flow are being priced for growth.
input_signals.reasoning: The reinvestment rate capx/max(oancf, dp) is itself a cross-theme quantity with no accounting double-count (capex is an investing-section item, never inside oancf), and flooring the denominator at depreciation removes the exploding scores that plague cash-flow-scaled ratios. Multiplying the two [0,1] ranks makes the signal high only for profitable non-reinvesters, so it is not the known FCF-to-assets or cash-based-profitability variable.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( ratio( capx, max( oancf, dp ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: outside_capital_per_internal_dollar
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3), 0.05), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(sstk, DELTA(dltt, 1)), MAX(oancf, dp)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Among firms that already generate solid internal cash, the amount of outside equity and debt raised per dollar of that internal cash reveals whether growth is being funded by an accommodating, optimistic market; profitable firms that need no external capital are underpriced, while profitable firms leaning heavily on issuance are overpriced growers.
input_signals.reasoning: The signal is switched on only where profitability is high, so it tests the specific channel that market optimism about profitable growers shows up as external funding, rather than adding a cash-profitability rank to a net-financing rank. Scaling external capital raised by internal cash generation (floored at depreciation) makes the two themes enter as one interacted quantity, and the zero-mean z-score leaves low-profitability firms neutral instead of contaminating the extremes.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ), 0.05 ), neg( zscore( winsor( ratio( add( sstk, delta( dltt, 1 ) ), max( oancf, dp ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: profitable_without_hiring
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(GROWTH(emp, 1), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Headcount growth is the least reversible and most expectation-driven form of investment; profitable firms that expand payroll aggressively are staffing up for growth the market already prices, while profitable firms holding employment flat are harvesting rents and returning cash.
input_signals.reasoning: Labor is a genuinely different investment channel from physical capex and is not spanned by CMA, so if the interaction is about managerial expansion appetite generally it should appear here too; if it only appears for capex, that tells us the mechanism is capital-specific. Employment growth is reported by nearly all firms, so coverage should exceed the cash-flow-based gates.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ma( ratio( oiadp, at ), 3 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( growth( emp, 1 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: persistent_cashcow_state_3y
input_signals.expression: MA(MUL(RANK(RATIO(oiadp, at)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), 1)))), 3)
input_signals.hypothesis: What is mispriced is not a one-year coincidence of high profit and low capacity growth but a persistent business model — a firm that has occupied the profitable-non-expander state for several consecutive years is a mature cash generator the market keeps discounting as if the rents were about to be competed away.
input_signals.reasoning: Smoothing the interaction score itself (rather than smoothing each input) rewards firms that stay in the joint quadrant, which should cut portfolio turnover and reduce the composition instability that likely weakened the gen-0 alphas. Gross PP&E growth is the cleanest measure of capacity expansion because, unlike net PP&E or total assets, it is not contaminated by depreciation or write-downs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ma( mul( rank( ratio( oiadp, at ) ), rank( neg( winsor( growth( ppegt, 1 ), 1 ) ) ) ), 3 )

input_signals.name: high_roic_capacity_harvester
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(oiadp, ppent), 1)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, dp), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms earning very high operating returns on their *installed* capital while spending less on capex than they book in depreciation are deliberately harvesting a high-return asset base; the market extrapolates the shrinking capacity as decaying earnings power and underprices the cash actually being released.
input_signals.reasoning: Neither leg is the archived construction: profitability is measured per dollar of installed physical capital (a capital-productivity concept, not ROA/RMW), and the investment leg is the capex-to-depreciation replacement ratio, which distinguishes maintenance from expansion rather than measuring size-scaled growth. The interaction is specifically "high return on old assets that are not being replaced," an economically different state from "profitable firm with slow asset growth."
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( winsor( ratio( oiadp, ppent ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( ratio( capx, dp ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: asset_light_margin_rents
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(ebitda, sale), 3)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ppent, sale), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Structural investment discipline is a *stock* property, not a growth rate: firms that sustain high operating margins while requiring very little fixed capital per dollar of sales have scalable rents with minimal future reinvestment needs, and book-anchored valuation systematically underprices such firms.
input_signals.reasoning: This contains no growth or change term at all, so it cannot be a double sort on RMW and CMA — the investment theme enters through capital intensity, which measures how much investment each future dollar of sales will *require* rather than how much was made last year. The economic claim is about the durability and capital-efficiency of rents, which is distinct from the harvesting story in the other proposals and gives the batch an independent lesson.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ma( ratio( ebitda, sale ), 3 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( ratio( ppent, sale ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: profit_weighted_expansion_penalty
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), ZSCORE(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(capx, aqc), LAG(ppent, 1)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Investment aggressiveness should be priced only where the market has something to extrapolate: among profitable firms, heavy capex-plus-acquisition spending relative to installed capital signals doubly-credited, overpriced growth, while among unprofitable firms investment intensity carries little valuation information.
input_signals.reasoning: The profitability rank enters as a bounded weight in [0,1] on a zero-mean investment-discipline z-score, so unprofitable firms are pulled toward the neutral middle instead of populating an extreme portfolio — this removes the reverse-RMW confound the critic identified while still making the short leg "profitable aggressive expanders" and the long leg "profitable harvesters." Using a continuous weight rather than an INDICATOR also avoids the point-mass problem that gave gen-0's `outside_capital_per_internal_dollar` a decent FMB slope but zero portfolio alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ma( ratio( oiadp, at ), 3 ) ), zscore( neg( winsor( ratio( add( capx, aqc ), lag( ppent, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: harvest_transition_reinvestment_drop
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(ebitda, at), 3)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(capx, MAX(ebitda, dp)), 1), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The repricing happens when a profitable firm *switches* from reinvesting to harvesting: a sharp fall in the share of internal cash flow being plowed back into capex, with profitability intact, signals a regime change to cash return that analysts extrapolate only slowly.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's best alpha came from the *level* of the reinvestment rate; this tests whether the newly-disciplined firm is priced even more slowly than the chronically disciplined one, which is a distinct state-change mechanism rather than a rescaling. Because the leg is a first difference of a cash-flow-normalized ratio, it has almost no overlap with CMA's asset-growth loading, which is what destroyed the growth-rate variants.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ma( ratio( ebitda, at ), 3 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( delta( ratio( capx, max( ebitda, dp ) ), 1 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: profitable_old_capital_base
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(ebitda, at), 3)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital vintage is investment discipline made visible on the balance sheet: a firm generating strong cash profits from a largely written-down asset base has been declining to replicate capacity for years, and the market discounts it for the capex bill it fears rather than valuing the rents it is currently extracting.
input_signals.reasoning: Net-to-gross PP&E is a stock measure of accumulated non-replacement, so it is orthogonal to one-year asset growth and to CMA, while capturing cumulative discipline better than any single-year flow. The interaction matters because old capital in an unprofitable firm signals obsolescence and distress, whereas old capital in a profitable firm signals a harvested franchise — only the joint state should predict returns.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ma( ratio( ebitda, at ), 3 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( ratio( ppent, ppegt ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: profitable_capex_own_history_low
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(oiadp, at), 3)), RANK(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Discipline should be judged against a firm's own investment norm, not the cross-section: a profitable firm currently spending at the bottom of its own five-year capex-intensity range has actively chosen to stop expanding, whereas a structurally low-capex firm is simply in a light industry.
input_signals.reasoning: TS_RANK makes the investment leg firm-demeaned by construction, which removes the industry and capital-intensity composition that appears to have neutralized the gen-1 harvester's alpha, while remaining a genuine investment-restraint measure. It also tests a different economic object than levels — managerial choice relative to own precedent — so the result is informative whichever way it goes.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ma( ratio( oiadp, at ), 3 ) ), rank( neg( ts_rank( ratio( capx, ppent ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: cash_yield_on_installed_capital_indadj
input_signals.expression: IND_ADJ(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oiadp, capx), ppent), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is the cash a firm actually releases from its existing plant: operating profit net of the capex needed to sustain or grow that plant, expressed per dollar of installed capital, and measured relative to industry peers who face the same technology and replacement needs.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than re-ranking the same two legs, this fuses profitability and investment into a single netted flow-per-capital-stock ratio, so a profitable heavy investor and an unprofitable non-investor can both score near zero — a structure no product of two ranks can produce. Industry-adjusting the level (not the ranks) removes the sector capital-intensity tilt that plausibly neutralized the gen-1 harvester's alpha while keeping a continuous, high-coverage signal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ind_adj( winsor( ratio( sub( oiadp, capx ), ppent ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: own_norm_profit_up_capex_down
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ebitda, at), MA(RATIO(ebitda, at), 5)), 1)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(capx, ppent), MA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The sharpest mispricing arises when a firm's profitability is running above its own historical norm while its capex is running below it: the windfall is real but management is not recycling it into capacity, so the cash must eventually reach shareholders — a state the market treats as unsustainable and discounts.
input_signals.reasoning: Making *both* legs deviations from the firm's own five-year norm produces a fully firm-demeaned interaction, which directly targets the failure mode we have diagnosed repeatedly (strong cross-sectional slopes killed by industry/style composition in the portfolio). It also changes the economic object from "profitable and disciplined levels" to "windfall not reinvested," a within-firm divergence no level-based archive member captures.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( winsor( sub( ratio( ebitda, at ), ma( ratio( ebitda, at ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( sub( ratio( capx, ppent ), ma( ratio( capx, ppent ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: joint_operating_capital_austerity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(xsga, sale), 1), 1))), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(RATIO(capx, sale), MA(RATIO(capx, sale), 5)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Genuine capital discipline usually travels with overhead discipline: a firm simultaneously cutting SG&A per sales dollar and investing below its own capex norm is executing a deliberate cash-harvest program, and the market misreads coordinated austerity as evidence of a shrinking franchise rather than of rising distributable cash.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the profitability *level* gate — which in several archive members turned into an RMW loading the FF5 benchmark absorbed — with a profitability *cost-side change*, so both legs are changes and neither is spanned by RMW or CMA. It tests a new economic construct, managerial austerity as a coordinated policy, rather than another profit-times-restraint level product.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( winsor( delta( ratio( xsga, sale ), 1 ), 1 ) ) ), rank( neg( winsor( ratio( ratio( capx, sale ), ma( ratio( capx, sale ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: profitable_expensed_not_capitalized_investment
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(ebitda, at), 3)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(xrd, ADD(capx, xrd)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is not only how much a firm invests but through which accounting channel: a profitable firm whose investment is predominantly expensed R&D rather than capitalized plant reports understated profitability and an understated asset base, so its true cash-generating capacity is systematically hidden from book-anchored valuation.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the financing-side leg the critic identified as a rediscovery with an investment-*composition* mechanism: the mix between expensed and capitalized investment, which affects measured profitability itself and therefore interacts with the profitability leg rather than sitting beside it. The ratio is continuous within the R&D-reporting population, avoiding the near-binary tie block that plagued the acquisition leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ma( ratio( ebitda, at ), 3 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( xrd, add( capx, xrd ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: cumulative_net_disinvestment_harvester
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(MA(RATIO(ebitda, at), 3)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(capx, dp), 5), ppegt), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year of low capex is noise; five consecutive years in which capex has cumulatively fallen short of depreciation means the firm has been shrinking real capacity for half a decade while remaining profitable, which identifies a mature franchise deliberately converting capital into cash.
input_signals.reasoning: The temporal object is different from anything tested: a five-year cumulative *net* capacity flow benchmarked against the gross capital stock, rather than a one-year capx/dp ratio (which gave a strong FMB slope but no alpha) or a position within own history (which is a relative measure with no notion of absolute shrinkage). Cumulating the capex-minus-depreciation gap also averages out the lumpy project timing that makes single-year capex ratios noisy, which should raise the reliability of the portfolio spread rather than just its magnitude.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ma( ratio( ebitda, at ), 3 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( ratio( ts_sum( sub( capx, dp ), 5 ), ppegt ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: idio_capex_restraint_vs_industry_cycle
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ebitda, at), MA(RATIO(ebitda, at), 5)), 1)), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(capx, ppent), MA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capex cuts are informative only when they are the firm's own decision rather than an industry-wide downturn: a profitable firm cutting investment below its own norm while its industry peers are not is revealing management's private view that expansion is no longer worth funding, and that idiosyncratic restraint is what the market fails to price.
input_signals.reasoning: Double-demeaning the investment leg — first against the firm's own five-year norm, then against the contemporaneous industry mean deviation — removes the common investment cycle that makes the raw own-norm leg partly a bet on sector capex booms and busts. This is a substantive economic distinction (idiosyncratic versus herd restraint), not a rescaling, and it directly targets the industry-composition problem we have diagnosed as the killer of FMB-strong/alpha-zero signals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( winsor( sub( ratio( ebitda, at ), ma( ratio( ebitda, at ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( ind_adj( winsor( sub( ratio( capx, ppent ), ma( ratio( capx, ppent ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: windfall_not_absorbed_by_inventory
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ebitda, at), MA(RATIO(ebitda, at), 5)), 1)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: If the mechanism is genuinely about not reinvesting a profit windfall, it should show up in working capital as well as in plant: a firm earning above its own profitability norm while carrying less inventory per sales dollar than its own norm is converting the windfall into cash rather than into stock on the shelf.
input_signals.reasoning: This holds the winning firm-demeaned structure fixed and changes only the asset category that could absorb the windfall, which answers whether the effect is capex-specific or a general operating-asset restraint mechanism. The cross-sectional inventory-to-sales change version delivered a weak +1.8% alpha at t=1.65, so the own-norm framing also tests whether firm-demeaning is what rescued the capex leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( winsor( sub( ratio( ebitda, at ), ma( ratio( ebitda, at ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( sub( ratio( invt, sale ), ma( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: windfall_without_labor_buildup
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ebitda, at), MA(RATIO(ebitda, at), 5)), 1)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(emp, sale), MA(RATIO(emp, sale), 5)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Labor is investment too: a firm earning above its own profitability norm while employing fewer people per sales dollar than its own norm is capturing rents through operating leverage rather than staffing up for anticipated growth, and that restraint should be rewarded in the same way as capital restraint.
input_signals.reasoning: The raw hiring-growth version was the archive's worst failure (α −2.9%, t −3.1), which we attribute to sorting on shrinking firms and to the CMA/labor-hiring style loading; replacing headcount growth with headcount *intensity relative to the firm's own norm* removes both the scale trend and the contraction bias while retaining the labor channel. This is a genuine repair test: if the labor channel now works, the earlier failure was construction rather than economics.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( winsor( sub( ratio( ebitda, at ), ma( ratio( ebitda, at ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( sub( ratio( emp, sale ), ma( ratio( emp, sale ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: harvest_screened_for_growing_revenue
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ebitda, at), MA(RATIO(ebitda, at), 5)), 1)), MIN(RANK(NEG(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(capx, ppent), MA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)), 1))), RANK(WINSOR(GROWTH(sale, 1), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A disciplined harvester must satisfy three conditions simultaneously — profitability above its own norm, capex below its own norm, and revenue still growing — because below-norm capex accompanied by falling revenue is contraction, not discipline, and only the former is underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: Nested MIN implements the screen the economics actually asks for: a large profitability deviation can no longer offset outright revenue contraction, since the score is capped by the weakest of the three ranks. This is a strict conjunction rather than the additive SUMRANK tilt, so the long portfolio is populated only by firms that jointly satisfy all three conditions and the sales-growth leg acts as a filter rather than as an independent growth bet.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( winsor( sub( ratio( ebitda, at ), ma( ratio( ebitda, at ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ), min( rank( neg( winsor( sub( ratio( capx, ppent ), ma( ratio( capx, ppent ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) ), rank( winsor( growth( sale, 1 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: pricing_power_without_expansion
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), MA(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 5)), 1)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(capx, ppent), MA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross margin running above a firm's own historical norm is direct evidence of pricing power or falling unit costs; when such a firm simultaneously invests below its own capex norm it is choosing to harvest the rent instead of expanding into it, and the market — which expects rents to be competed away or reinvested — underprices the resulting cash flow.
input_signals.reasoning: The two legs now share no accounting inputs: the profitability side is built from sales and cost of goods sold, while the investment side is capex over net PP&E, which eliminates the mechanical denominator overlap that made the utilization version a doubled low-investment bet. Gross margin is also a cleaner measure of product-market rents than EBITDA-to-assets, so this tests a distinct economic source of the harvestable cash flow.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( winsor( sub( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), sale ), ma( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), sale ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( sub( ratio( capx, ppent ), ma( ratio( capx, ppent ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: restraint_where_capital_matters
input_signals.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ebitda, at), MA(RATIO(ebitda, at), 5)), 1)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(capx, ppent), MA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)), 1)))), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ppent, at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A capex decision only releases meaningful cash where capital is a large share of the business: in heavy-asset firms a below-norm capex year frees a substantial fraction of enterprise cash flow, while in asset-light firms the same deviation is economically trivial, so the mispricing should be concentrated among capital-intensive harvesters.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a moderation hypothesis — effect size scaling with capital intensity — and it deliberately runs against the archive's `asset_light_margin_rents` result (α +2.7%), so the two outcomes are jointly informative about whether the harvest story or an asset-light quality story drives the family. The third factor enters as a bounded rank weight, so it concentrates rather than replaces the interaction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( mul( rank( winsor( sub( ratio( ebitda, at ), ma( ratio( ebitda, at ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( sub( ratio( capx, ppent ), ma( ratio( capx, ppent ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( ppent, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: shift_from_capacity_to_innovation
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ebitda, at), MA(RATIO(ebitda, at), 5)), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(xrd, ADD(capx, xrd)), MA(RATIO(xrd, ADD(capx, xrd)), 5)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Discipline is not the same as inactivity: a profitable firm shifting its investment mix away from capitalized capacity and toward expensed R&D depresses its own reported earnings and book assets while building unrecognized capital, so its true profitability is understated exactly when its measured profitability is already improving.
input_signals.reasoning: The level version of this mix produced the second-highest FMB slope in the archive (4.02) with α +2.2% at t 1.90, and recasting it as an own-norm shift tests whether the pricing information is in the static composition or in the reallocation decision. It is the one remaining channel where "low capex" should be rewarded for a reason unrelated to harvesting, which makes it a genuine discriminating test of the family's mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( winsor( sub( ratio( ebitda, at ), ma( ratio( ebitda, at ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( sub( ratio( xrd, add( capx, xrd ) ), ma( ratio( xrd, add( capx, xrd ) ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: moat_conditioned_harvest
input_signals.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), MA(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 5)), 1)), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(capx, ppent), MA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)), 1))))), RANK(IND_ADJ(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Only a firm with a genuine competitive advantage can stop investing without losing its franchise: harvesting is value-creating when the firm's gross margin stands above its industry peers' (a moat), whereas identical restraint by a below-peer-margin firm is capex starvation in a losing position and should not be rewarded.
input_signals.reasoning: The third factor here is industry-relative margin *level* — a competitive-position measure that has never been evaluated in this archive — rather than the sales-growth screen, so this is not a restacking of already-tested components but a new moderating economic condition on the harvest mechanism.
